evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Fraxinus berlandieriana and lists Texas within its native range.
Travis County — modern taxonomic work documents both F. berlandieriana and F. pennsylvanica collected in Travis County and discusses the Travis/Bastrop disjunction.
Comal County — Nesom's treatment designates Lindheimer 653 from Comal County as the lectotype of a synonym now within F. berlandieriana.
Regional sources place the species on the eastern/southern Edwards Plateau and in San Antonio/Nueces watershed riparian systems, but those broader statements are not converted into extra counties.
target_zone_range.blocking_issue: Only two target counties are firm enough under the project's exact-county rule. Regional evidence strongly indicates additional target-zone occurrence, but B014 does not infer Bexar, Medina or Uvalde without county-level documentation.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Historic confusion with F. pennsylvanica and F. velutina is well documented. Identification should rely on leaflet number/serration, leaf scar, and especially samara structure, including occasional 3-winged fruits.

morphology.look_here_first: Count leaflets and inspect the fruit: Mexican ash usually has 3–5 leaflets with coarse sharp serration on the distal half, plus a samara whose wings gradually expand from near the base; some trees produce a few distinctive 3-winged fruits.
diagnostic_traits: medium riparian/bottomland ash of southern and central Texas
usually 3–5(–7) leaflets, fewer on average than green ash
leaflet margins coarsely and sharply serrate on distal half to two-thirds
lower leaflet surface glabrous in the Central Texas comparison key
leaf scar shallowly hemispheric, about 2.2–3 mm wide, apex shallowly concave
samaras usually 2-winged but occasional 3-winged fruits may occur on the same tree
wings gradually expand from the base toward distal third and narrowly flange the fruit body

confusers.separator: Green ash generally has 5–7(9) less-coarsely-serrate leaflets, a broader shield-shaped scar, and consistently 2-winged samaras whose wings broaden more abruptly.
Texas ash usually has 5–7 leaflets, a glaucous white-waxy lower surface, and a much smaller samara body with a mostly terminal wing.
Velvet ash has a western distribution and can overlap morphologically; taxonomic history contains misidentified/intermediate material, so locality and reproductive characters matter.

installation_guardrail: Do not install as a project-native until the three-county evidence requirement is met or Calvin explicitly approves a documented exception.
